title: Generic pure-private online learning against oblivious adversaries
formal: Historical question, resolved positively: does every binary hypothesis class H of finite representation dimension admit, for each fixed ε>0, a pure ε-differentially private online learner with o(T) expected prediction mistakes on every realizable length-T sequence fixed by an oblivious adversary? The learner may know T, may output hypotheses outside H, and has no computational-efficiency requirement.
context:
Each prediction hypothesis can reveal something about earlier training examples. The privacy budget here protects one changed example in the joint distribution of all hypotheses released during the T rounds.

The original paper asks whether one can go beyond constructions for particular classes. The answer covers every class of finite representation dimension, including infinite classes. Finite Littlestone dimension alone is not the hypothesis of this pure-privacy theorem.

An oblivious adversary fixes its sequence before observing the learner’s random outputs. The same paper proves an obstruction for adaptive adversaries even for an infinite point-function class. Its generic positive result therefore does not establish the adaptive version.

A polylogarithmic number of expected mistakes grows with T, but its fraction of all T predictions tends to zero. This is enough for the source’s online-learnability criterion; the theorem does not promise efficient computation or a T-independent mistake bound.
why: Connects pure private PAC learnability to sequential prediction and identifies how the adversary’s access to the learner’s outputs changes that connection.
status_note: Resolved by Li, Wang and Ye, NeurIPS 2024, Theorem 3.3. references.title: On the Growth of Mistakes in Differentially Private Online Learning: A Lower Bound Perspective
references.authors: Daniil Dmitriev, Kristóf Szabó, Amartya Sanyal

definitions: Let X be an instance domain and H⊆{0,1}^X. Before learning starts, an oblivious adversary fixes h*∈H and x_1,…,x_T∈X, with labels y_t=h*(x_t). In round t the randomized learner outputs a hypothesis h_t:X→{0,1} using only its previous observations, then receives (x_t,y_t); its mistake count is Σ_t 1[h_t(x_t)≠y_t]. The guarantee is a worst-case bound on the expectation over the learner’s randomness. Pure ε-differential privacy means that for any two length-T labeled sequences S,S′ differing in one example and any event E of full output sequences, Pr[A(S)∈E]≤e^ε Pr[A(S′)∈E]. This privacy condition applies to all labeled sequences, including unrealizable ones. A probabilistic representation of H is a distribution P over finite sets V of binary hypotheses such that, for every h*∈H and every distribution D on X, with probability at least 3/4 over V∼P some v∈V has Pr_{x∼D}[v(x)≠h*(x)]≤1/4. Its size is the largest log|V| in its support, and RepDim(H) is the infimum of these sizes. Finite representation dimension is the class condition characterizing pure private PAC learnability. The target o(T) is for each fixed H and ε as T tends to infinity, uniformly over the realizable oblivious sequences; it does not mean a finite mistake bound independent of T.
answer_criterion: The published affirmative theorem establishes an ε-private learner with expected mistake bound O(log²T·(RepDim(H)+log log T)²/ε) for large T, which is o(T) for every fixed finite RepDim(H) and ε>0. The result is information-theoretic and applies to oblivious realizable sequences.
